title: Circular Array Loop
description:
# Circular Array Loop

You are given a circular array `nums` of non-zero integers. If you are at index `i`, then `nums[i]` tells you how many steps to move:

* A positive value moves forward.
* A negative value moves backward.

Moving past either end wraps around to the other side of the array. For example, in an array of length `n`, the next index after moving from `i` is `((i + nums[i]) % n + n) % n`.

Return `true` if there is a valid cycle; otherwise return `false`. A cycle is valid only if both conditions hold:

* Its length is greater than `1`. A move that returns from an index directly to itself is not a valid cycle.
* Every number used by the cycle has the same sign, so every move in the cycle goes in the same direction.

## Example 1:

**Input:** nums = [2,-1,1,2,2]
**Output:** true
**Explanation:** Indices `0 -> 2 -> 3 -> 0` form a cycle of length `3`, and all moves in that cycle are forward.

## Example 2:

**Input:** nums = [-1,2]
**Output:** false
**Explanation:** Index `1` moves back to itself because `2` is a multiple of the array length, but a one-index self loop is not a valid cycle.

## Example 3:

**Input:** nums = [-2,1,-1,-2,-2]
**Output:** false
**Explanation:** Any repeating path either changes direction or collapses into an invalid one-index loop.

## Constraints:

* `1 <= nums.length <= 5000`
* `-1000 <= nums[i] <= 1000`
* `nums[i] != 0`

## Follow up:

Could you solve it in `O(n)` time complexity and `O(1)` extra space complexity?

solutions.name: Fast and Slow Pointers with In-Place Marking
solutions.description:
## Approach

For each index that has not already been cleared, run Floyd's fast and slow pointers while the path keeps the same sign. If the pointers meet, reject the case where the meeting index points to itself; otherwise a valid cycle exists. After a failed start, walk the same-direction path again and set those entries to `0` so they are never processed again.

## Key Insight

A valid cycle is exactly a same-direction cycle of length greater than one. In-place marking is safe because the original constraints exclude zero, so zero can mean "already proven not useful".

## Complexity Analysis

Each index is cleared at most once. Time Complexity: O(n). Space Complexity: O(1).

solutions.name: Visited Color Array Traversal
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use a color id for each starting traversal. Follow the path while the direction matches the start and the current index has no color. If the path reaches an index colored by the current traversal, measure the cycle length by walking once around it; return true only when the length is greater than one.

## Key Insight

The color id separates "visited in this path" from "visited by an older path". That distinction is enough to identify a same-path cycle without a hash map.

## Complexity Analysis

Every index receives a color at most once. Time Complexity: O(n). Space Complexity: O(n).

solutions.name: Path Index Map Detection
solutions.description:
## Approach

For each unprocessed start, follow the path while all numbers keep the same sign. A map records each index's position inside the current path. Revisiting a mapped index proves a same-direction cycle, while checking `next == index` rejects one-index self loops before they can count.

## Key Insight

The map makes the current path explicit. It is not the lowest-memory route, but it is useful for teaching exactly where the repeated segment begins.

## Complexity Analysis

Each index becomes processed after at most one path exploration. Time Complexity: O(n). Space Complexity: O(n).

solutions.name: Timestamped Path Arrays
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use two arrays instead of a hash map: `seenAt[index]` stores the traversal stamp that first saw an index, and `depth[index]` stores its order in that traversal. While following one same-direction path, revisiting an index with the current stamp gives the cycle length as `step - depth[index]`.

## Key Insight

This is the array version of path-index detection. It keeps the "where did this path repeat" information while avoiding per-path map allocation.

## Complexity Analysis

Every finished path marks its indices as done. Time Complexity: O(n). Space Complexity: O(n).
